Rust for Project Intent: How AFWE Caught Its Own Blindspot

Rust made memory mistakes impossible to make quietly. AFWE makes regressions of intent impossible to make quietly. Inside the post-mortem of how silent capability severance slipped through—and the deterministic ratchets that now prevent it.

AFWE Core Architecture Team • October 27, 2026 • 8 min read

"Rust for project intent." Rust made memory mistakes impossible to make quietly. AFWE makes regressions of intent impossible to make quietly.

The chair

Ask an agent to build a chair, and while it works it decides to add adjustable arms. That is a reasonable call, and it is now part of the chair. Two weeks later you ask for a completely new design. The agent looks at the new chair, decides adjustable arms don't belong, and drops them. It may even be right.

The problem is that nobody decided that. The arms disappeared as a side effect of a rewrite, and you find out three weeks later when someone asks where they went.

AFWE doesn't take a side on whether the arms should stay. It takes notes. When the new design removes something that an earlier decision created, AFWE stops and asks you to say so: yes, no adjustable arms, that is deliberate. If you later change your mind, the old code is in git, linked to the decision that created it, down to the individual functions. Bringing the arms back is a lookup, not a rebuild.

You could always do this by hand. The difference is cost. Without AFWE, finding out what you are about to lose means a week of digging through chat history and thousands of tokens, so almost nobody does it. AFWE shows you at the moment of the change, when you can still act on it.

When AFWE failed on its own code

During dogfooding on the ReBorn branch, an agent retired the legacy v1 workflows in turn t0022. It removed the CLI call to contract::task_start, but crates/afwe-core/src/contract.rs was never touched. The function went dead, and the commit gate passed.

In the same stretch, briefing logic was duplicated inside turn.begin instead of reusing context::scope_matches. The tool built to stop silent architectural decay had let both through in its own engine.

We stopped feature work and ran a post-mortem instead of patching the symptom with a better prompt.

Why touched-file checks miss it

Most verification inspects only the files a change modified. A function rarely goes dead because someone deleted the function. It goes dead because someone deleted its caller, and the caller lives in a different file.

Turn t0022 diff:
  M crates/afwe-cli/src/main.rs        (call to contract::task_start removed)
    crates/afwe-core/src/contract.rs   (untouched, 0 bytes changed)

Gate verdict: PASSED

The callee's file had no diff, so the gate never looked at it. Cross-module severance is invisible to any check that starts from the diff.

The fix: two ratchets

Both ratchets are deterministic. The same repository state gives the same verdict, whether a human or an agent made the change.

  • Decision-to-code links are what linters cannot do, because they know nothing about intent. Active decisions, pinned invariants and docs are linked to files and symbols.
  • Inbound-reference counts compare how often each exported symbol is referenced across the whole workspace, at turn begin and at turn commit. This catches a callee going dead even when its own file was never touched.
Verdict Fires when
ORPHANED_DECISION A symbol, file or node tied to an active decision vanishes with no explicit supersede or update
ORPHANED_PIN A pinned invariant loses the code that implements it
DOCS_DRIFT Documentation links point at deleted code
SEVERED_CAPABILITY An exported symbol drops from more than 0 references to 0
DEAD_ON_ARRIVAL A new exported symbol in a touched file is born with 0 references

Existing dead code is grandfathered in a baseline file, so the gate blocks only what a turn newly breaks. Without that, the first run on an established repo flags hundreds of old functions and people turn the tool off.

The over-approximation policy

A syntax parser cannot tell which run() a call like engine.run() refers to. So AFWE counts any identifier occurrence as a reference. Errors then fall in one direction only: it may miss some dead code, and it should not flag live code.

The cost is that generic names such as new, len, run and get can never be flagged. Dynamic dispatch, string lookups and macro registration are also treated as references. So the honest claim is narrower than "impossible": a regression to an exported, non-generic symbol across modules can't happen quietly.

Roots such as main.rs, lib.rs and test directories are inferred by fixed rules, and editing them by hand requires a recorded reason, the same as changing a pin. Otherwise an agent could silence the gate by declaring its dead function a root.

What we decided not to build

A gate that tries to do everything becomes a slow, noisy pseudo-compiler. These three ideas were considered and cut:

  • Struct fields and enum variants. Many are populated only through deserialization (Serde, Pydantic, Jackson), so a static reference count sees them as never used. Compilers and linters already handle the private cases. AFWE stays at the capability level: module, type, function, contract, decision.
  • Signature diffs on every exported function. Agents change internal signatures dozens of times an hour. Requiring a declaration for each one trains them to declare everything. Breaking-change checks apply only at real boundaries: crate exports, CLI commands, tool schemas and RPC contracts.
  • Undeclared roots. Hardcoding main.rs as the only root would flag benchmarks, migration scripts and handlers as dead. Roots are inferred by fixed rules, written to the manifest, and changes to them need a reason.

Where a language's compiler already covers a check, AFWE defers to it. That boundary moves by language. Python has no compiler doing this work, so AFWE has to do more there.

What a pass means

A pass from AFWE means the change is consistent with the intent that was recorded. It does not mean the code is correct.

Rust's borrow checker is a proof for its domain: safe Rust cannot have a use-after-free. AFWE is not a proof. Its graph over-approximates, and the assumptions it records were written by a model and may be wrong. What AFWE guarantees is that the record is faithful to what was captured, that every later change is checked against it, and that a contradiction is surfaced instead of buried.

The model is free to propose anything. The gate's verdict comes only from data and rules a human can read and re-run.

See it catch t0022

The demo script reproduces the failure. Run it on Linux or macOS, or in PowerShell on Windows: 

./scripts/demo.sh
.\scripts\demo.ps1

In step 3 it edits checkout.ts to remove the call to charge2, leaving charge.ts untouched. The commit gate stops it:

> afwe turn commit t0003
REDO: t0003 NOT committed
  SEVERED_CAPABILITY: 'src/payments/charge.ts::charge2' lost all incoming callers (dropped from 1 to 0). Restore the caller, wire it in, or declare it in turn assume with action remove or replace.

The gate clears once the intent is declared, which puts the decision on the record: 

{
  "intents": [
    { "id": "decouple-charge", "action": "update", "targets": ["payments"] },
    { "id": "deprecate-charge2", "action": "replace", "targets": ["src/payments/charge.ts"] }
  ]
}

What "quietly" means

Rust doesn't stop you from writing unsafe. It makes you write the word, so the risk is visible and local. AFWE treats intent the same way. You can retire a capability, delete a module or cross an architectural boundary. You just have to say so in turn assume, with a reason, and the decision goes on the record.

What you can no longer do is lose something because a model forgot what was agreed three turns ago. Overrides are a visible escape hatch, and a project that overrides everything is easy to spot.

You can break things on purpose. You can't break them by accident.
